specAnchors.text: know that a catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction, but is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction
know that a catalyst works by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy

primer.text: From Explaining Rates you already know why hotter, denser crowds of particles react faster. This note introduces the helper that speeds reactions without being consumed, the catalyst, and the alternative pathway that explains its power. Industrial chemistry leans on these substances every day.

modules.title: What a catalyst is and is not
sourceHeadings: The effect of a catalyst on rate of reaction
modules.opening: A catalyst is chemistry's helper that is not used up: it speeds the reaction and walks away unchanged. This lesson pins down the definition, the small amounts needed and the way catalysts appear above reaction arrows.
keyPoints: A catalyst raises the rate of a reaction yet finishes it chemically unchanged.
Catalysts speed up reactions without themselves being altered or consumed.
Only small amounts of a catalyst are normally needed to have an effect.
Weigh a catalyst before and after a reaction and its mass reads exactly the same.
Catalysts are written above or below the reaction arrow rather than in the equation.

low.restatement: A catalyst makes a reaction faster but comes out of the reaction exactly as it went in, so a tiny pinch can serve again and again. Its name is never listed with the reactants, only over the arrow.
low.analogy: It is like a matchmaker at a wedding: the pairing happens faster, but the matchmaker leaves exactly as they arrived.
low.examPointer: Quote both halves of the definition: faster rate and chemically unchanged at the end.

medium.restatement: Catalysts raise the rate of a reaction while remaining chemically unchanged, so their mass is identical before and after. Small amounts suffice, and the catalyst is shown above the reaction arrow because it is not a reactant or product.
medium.analogy: A catalyst behaves like a revolving door: crowds pass through much faster, yet the door itself neither joins the crowd nor wears out.
medium.examPointer: Mention the unchanged mass and the arrow notation when justifying why a catalyst is not in the equation.

modules.title: How catalysts work and where industry uses them
sourceHeadings: The effect of a catalyst on rate of reaction
modules.opening: The shortcut is the secret: a catalyst offers the reaction an alternative pathway with a lower energy hurdle. This lesson walks that mechanism and meets the industrial catalysts built on it.
keyPoints: A catalyst opens a lower-energy route that lets more collisions succeed.
Different processes need different catalysts, but all work on the same principle.
Catalysts attract reactant molecules onto their surface, providing a lower-energy route.
Catalysis raises production rates and reduces energy costs in commercial chemistry.
Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.

low.restatement: Instead of the steep hill the reaction normally climbs, a catalyst opens a gentler path, so more particles can make the journey. The same idea serves every industry, and living cells use it too through enzymes.
low.analogy: It is like a mountain road tunnelling through the pass: the summit stays the same, but far more lorries can make the crossing.
low.examPointer: Use the phrase alternative pathway with lower activation energy when explaining how catalysts work.

medium.restatement: A catalyst opens an easier route whose lower energy hurdle lets a greater proportion of collisions succeed, so the rate rises. Atoms on the catalyst surface attract reactant molecules, and the same principle spans industrial processes and the enzymes of living systems.
medium.analogy: A ferry turns a long drive around the bay into a short crossing; the destination is unchanged, but the journey is easier and far more traffic completes it.
medium.examPointer: Link the lowered barrier to more successful collisions, then name surface action and enzymes as extensions.

glossary.definition: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end.
The minimum energy particles need for a reaction to occur; catalysts open a lower pathway.
The easier reaction route that a catalyst provides, with a lower energy barrier.
A biological molecule that acts as a catalyst in living systems.
A block of metals widely used as catalysts because they donate and accept electrons readily.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the full definition of a catalyst. b) Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. c) 2.00 g of manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution; at the end the solid is filtered off, dried and re-weighed. State its expected mass and what this shows.
steps: a) A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.
b) It provides an alternative pathway for the reaction with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions succeed and the rate rises.

c) The mass reads 2.00 g again: a catalyst's mass is identical before and after, showing it is not consumed — small amounts suffice, and it is written above the reaction arrow rather than in the equation.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Speeds up the reaction, chemically unchanged at the end. b) Alternative pathway with lower activation energy. c) 2.00 g — unchanged, so not consumed.
